title: GenTile: Closing the Loop Between LLM Reasoning and Physical Telemetry for Autonomous NPU Graph Tuning
abstract: Abstract Large language model (LLM) hidden widths—such as the 18 944-dimensional intermediate layer of the Qwen family—are often burst-aligned but not tile-compatible with heterogeneous NPU Cube engines, forcing the compiler to emit a small residual kernel that stalls the pipeline for up to 77% of cycles. Manual tuning does not scale across the growing space of model dimensions, sequence lengths, and operator variants. We present GenTile, a dual-role Research–Development (R&D) agent framework that closes the loop between LLM causal reasoning and on-device telemetry: a Research agent diagnoses bottlenecks from structured profiles, a Development agent materializes hardware-legal descriptors from compiler feedback, and iteration traces accumulate into a reusable knowledge base under an air-gap sandbox. On Ascend 910B, an offline hardware-faithful sandbox loop first demonstrates convergence mechanics; on real pretrained weights, the loop then measures the full multi-objective trade-off—latency, energy, memory, AICore efficiency, and approximation error (ε)—across six projection families from two Qwen generations (Qwen3.5-32B and Qwen2.5-7B). From telemetry alone, the agent deploys lossless sibling-projection fusions (QKV, gate–up) consistent with production inference-engine layouts (1.06–1.16× faster, up to 13% lower energy, ε=0, stable across sequence lengths, layer depths, and both models), and rejects every lossy low-rank rewrite—including a 1.39× lm_head speedup whose measured ε=0.89 exceeds any usable accuracy budget—while validating the Eckart–Young cliff prediction (ε → 0.002 at the tail rank) on structural layers. Baselines, ablations, cross-dimension generalization, and a sandbox loop that matches the geometric Oracle within four generations without exhaustive search further support the framework.

title: When Does Mixing Models Pay? Open Fusion, a Bounded Mixture-of-Agents Runtime, and Registered Evidence from Local Coding Benchmarks
abstract: Mixture-of-Agents (MoA) methods combine the outputs of several large language models (LLMs) at inference time and have reported gains on conversational benchmarks. Whether those gains survive deployment constraints — fixed call budgets, local hardware, objective grading and fair same-model baselines — is less clear. I present OpenFusion, an open-source, OpenAI-compatible runtime that implements fourteen bounded multi-model strategies, from fallback and Self-MoA to semantic voting, rank-then-fuse, layered refinement and uncertainty cascades, under a hard per-request call ceiling. It ships with an evaluation laboratory that reports Wilson intervals, paired tests, order-balanced judging and panel-complementarity diagnostics.Using the project's published artifacts, I report a series of local studies on two NVIDIA GB10 workstations with 4B-parameter open models. In a registered prospective study on 500 previously unused MBPP tasks, a fixed test-guided mixed-model workflow passed 78.1% of all-test evaluations versus 72.5% for repeated same-model repair (+5.6 points, 95% CI [3.6, 7.7]), with 17.2% lower mean latency and 29.2% fewer tokens. A confidence-gated escalation policy raised held-out accuracy on a 70-item programmatic benchmark from 75.7% to 91.4% while calling a stronger model on 40% of items.Five later controls, however, did not show that model diversity itself causes the gains. Against fresh sampling from the same model, mixed panels tied or underperformed: −0.57 points on 1,500 tasks, and −5.0 points after a 32-policy development search. I conclude that, in this setting, the measurable benefit of MoA-style systems comes from verification, bounded retries and selective escalation rather than from mixing similarly sized models. I close with a five-step selection rule and a reporting checklist for practitioners.
journal: Journal of Artificial Intelligence & Cloud Computing

title: Autonomous Agents Based on Large Language Models: Reasoning Strategies and Multi-Agent Interaction
abstract: Language-model agents acquire capability along two routes that published work almost always varies together, one enlarging the computation a single agent performs and the other enlarging the number of agents and the channels along which they pass partial results, which leaves the contribution of each route indistinguishable. This paper separates an agent system into a reasoning operator and an interaction topology, holding the number of agents fixed at three across all multi-agent topologies, together with the number of rounds, the message cap, the prompt skeleton, and the memory settings for all combinations, and evaluates a full factorial design of four reasoning levels and four topologies on three public test sets totalling 484 instances under five random seeds, giving 38,720 task executions. Comparisons are paired at the instance level, and effects are estimated from logistic mixed-effects models fitted to each test set separately. The reasoning factor spans 18.0 points on the static suite whereas the topology factor spans 7.8 points on the interactive one, a reversal indicating that the two mechanisms act on different failure modes. The topology span is taken across all four topology levels and therefore includes the step from one agent to three, against a structure-only span of 2.8 points among the multi-agent topologies. The two factors also depart from additivity in a localised manner. A mechanism-motivated single-degree-of-freedom contrast on the only cell in which both factors contribute a corrective pass is significant at p = 0.001 on the static suite, whereas the omnibus nine-degree-of-freedom interaction test is not (p = 0.094), and in that cell the observed 50.0 percent lies 5.8 points below the additive expectation. After tokens are counted, seven of the sixteen configurations remain undominated on the static suite and five on the operating-system suite, and returns saturate at 12,400 tokens per instance on the static suite under the present design.

title: Online LLM Inference Routing for Multi-Agent Systems under Long-Term Budget and Layered Privacy Constraints
abstract: Abstract The Cloud-Edge-End (CEE) collaborative architecture has become a key paradigm for deploying highly intelligent multi-agent systems with low latency and high energy efficiency. Existing studies on efficient task offloading in CEE, however, either overlook long-term financial budget constraints from commercial API token usage and edge computing leasing, or inadequately handle layered information-sharing and privacy restrictions in decentralized autonomous agents. This paper investigates online inference routing to minimize the computational and communication overhead of large language model (LLM) workloads under long-term budget constraints, agent intent-sharing limitations, and un-known future prompt lengths. We propose a budget-aware online optimization framework that uses Lyapunov optimization to decouple long-term financial constraints, and show that the decoupled problem forms a generalized ordinal potential game. To address heterogeneous information-sharing restrictions, we design an adaptive best response algorithm for cooperative environments with shared decision information, and a multi-agent distributed routing algorithm for limited-information environments, enabling efficient offloading without inter-agent intent sharing. Theoretical analysis provides conditional performance and queue-length bounds and establishes finite convergence of the per-slot solvers. Simulations on distributed inference testbeds show that our scheme reduces the inference overhead of heterogeneous agentic tasks while achieving a favorable trade-off between performance and actual token expenditure.

title: Instruction-tuning large language models with medical classification data improves ICD coding of German tumor diagnoses
abstract: Abstract Accurate coding of tumor diagnoses, with the German Modification of the International Classification of Diseases, 10th Revision (ICD-10-GM), and the International Classification of Diseases for Oncology, Third Edition (ICD-O-3), is essential for structured cancer documentation. Large language models (LLMs) offer opportunities for automating such tasks, but locally deployable, open-weight models often lack sufficient domain-specific coding expertise. This study investigates whether instruction-based fine-tuning on public classification resources improves the coding accuracy of open-weight LLMs for German tumor diagnosis texts. Eight models from the Qwen, Llama, and Mistral families (7–70 billion parameters) were fine-tuned on over 500,000 question-answer pairs based on the ICD-10-GM, ICD-O-3, and German procedure classification. The evaluation uses coded diagnoses from the local tumor documentation system as test data. ICD-10-GM accuracy rose from 1.4 to 24 to 41–58%, and partial (three-character codes only) accuracy from 31 to 74 to 73–83%. The accuracy of ICD-O-3 topography coding also improved but started and remained considerably lower. Malformed code outputs dropped to nearly 0% for almost all models. Tumor-diagnosis recognition reached 99%. A data quality analysis showed that incomplete diagnosis descriptions limited achievable test performance. Accuracy correlated positively with model size, but gaps between small and large models narrowed after fine-tuning. The reasoning mode in Qwen3 generally yielded lower performance than fine-tuning and was over 100 times slower. Our findings highlight the potential of leveraging public catalogues to build instruction datasets that improve LLMs in medical documentation tasks. To support reproducibility and further research, we publicly release the complete training dataset and the best-performing fine-tuned model checkpoints.

title: A STUDY OF GENERATIVE AI TOOLS IN EDUCATION
abstract: The integration of Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) into educational ecosystems marks a structural paradigm shift in pedagogical design, instructional delivery, and learner assessment. Driven by rapid advancements in Large Language Models (LLMs) and multimodal foundational architectures, AI tools have transformed from specialized sequence-labelling utilities into interactive, highly adaptable cognitive co-processors1. This paper presents a comprehensive study of Generative AI tools in education, investigating their theoretical pedagogical foundations, empirical effectiveness in technical and computer application disciplines, assessment redesign dynamics, institutional governance policies, and ethical challenges. Grounded in the SAMR model, Bloom's Taxonomy, and Intelligent-TPACK frameworks, we analyse how generative tools shift student learning from passive syntax creation to high-order code evaluation and systems reasoning. Empirical findings from computer science education demonstrate that "Open-but-Verify" operational frameworks and "Prompt Problems" effectively preserve learning outcomes while leveraging AI efficiency. Finally, this paper evaluates institutional policy diffusion and the SPADE ethical framework (Sustainability, Privacy, Digital divide, and Ethics) to establish guidelines for sustainable AI integration in higher education curricula.

title: Social-HUMINT: An LLM-Augmented Unified Framework for Measuring Social Media Exposure
abstract: In the post-API landscape, social-media profiling has become inexpensive and automated: Large Language Models (LLMs) can extract structured information from unstructured content and deduce attributes users never disclosed. A person's true exposure is not what they post but what can be inferred from it. As these practices become routine, exposure to social engineering attacks becomes an operational certainty, demanding a shared framework for assessment and mitigation. We make this exposure measurable by quantifying how accurately a target can be profiled, and how far that profile enables social engineering attacks. Because no existing model fully spans this continuum, we unify Social Media Intelligence (SOCMINT) and Cyber Human Intelligence (Cyber-HUMINT), two individual-focused disciplines that evolved separately, into a single doctrine-grounded taxonomy of 38 capabilities across the Cyber Threat Intelligence lifecycle, where user profiling bridges passive collection and active engagement. Domain experts validated the taxonomy (Fleiss' $κ$ = 0.92). We operationalize its core path (extraction, inference, and susceptibility assessment) as an LLM-augmented multi-agent pipeline, evaluated on real participants' public data. Susceptibility is assessed indirectly: the pipeline predicts how each target would rank personalized engagement options, matching their actual choices significantly above chance. This ranking capacity captures the personalization on which tailored attacks depend. The underlying profiles are accurate: extraction reaches F1 = 97.3%, and inferred attributes score 4.73/5, both far above rule-based and NER-based baselines at negligible cost. The framework augments security analysts' tradecraft rather than replacing it and enables defenders to gauge their own exposure before an adversary does.

title: Certified Execution Harness for Agentic AI: Safe and Least-Intrusive Petri-Net Supervisory Control Between Reasoning and Action
abstract: This paper studies the problem of safe tool execution for large language model (LLM) agents under prompt injection. Using Petri nets, we formalize the execution harness between the LLM and its tools as a supervisory control problem, in which marks represent capabilities, approvals and budgets. Since a transition fires only if the marks it needs are present, an injected request whose preconditions are unmet or already spent is refused regardless of its wording. Treating tool outcomes as uncontrollable, we enforce safety by the conventional maximally permissive supervisor, and this safety transfers to the running system under four assumptions. Moreover, to capture an agent that may propose again after a refusal, we introduce the notion of a replanning closed loop, in which each retry costs an inference call. We show that, in this loop, the conventional supervisor can be arbitrarily more intrusive than a stricter safe one. Furthermore, for a given proposer model, the maximally permissive least-intrusive supervisor is characterized as a value-threshold refinement of the conventional one. Under precise conditions, this refinement orders two concurrent actions by at most one monitor place. On an autonomous release agent, we find by synthesis that safe deployment requires a step that the supervisor can refuse after a rollout starts.

Using Petri nets, we formalize the execution harness between the LLM and its tools as a supervisory control problem, in which marks represent capabilities, approvals and budgets.

title: Consistent but Biased: Chair Personas Trade Noise for Bias in Multi-Agent Clinical Decisions
abstract: In clinical systems built from several large language model (LLM) agents, one agent often chairs the discussion and makes the final decision. Whether the chair's persona prompt changes that decision, or the agreement between repeated runs that some systems treat as reliability, has not been tested with the case held constant. We ask whether the persona changes the decision or only its timing, how it affects agreement between runs, and which behaviors appear when the prompt describes only personality traits. A simulated department of seven agents discussed 20 published cases of degenerative cervical myelopathy, with the case reports replayed unchanged in every run. Only the prompts of the chair and its deputy changed (no persona, or a consultative, autocratic or avoidant one), written either as rules of conduct or as personality traits. With personas written as rules, the chair chose to operate now in 93% of runs when autocratic and in 2% when avoidant, against 57% without a persona. Surgery was still planned in nearly all decisions, so the personas mainly changed whether to operate now or after more tests. These effects held with a second model and reworded prompts. The autocratic and avoidant personas made the three runs of a case agree more often, but only about as often as chance predicts, and Fleiss $κ$ did not rise. Prompts that described only personality traits kept more than half of the autocratic and avoidant effects on operating now. They reproduced quick decisions, delays and extra tests, but not ignoring red flags, dropping backup plans or passing the decision to the family. Studies should report and vary the chair's persona as they do the model, and correct agreement between runs for chance before calling it reliability.

title: Trion-1: Unifying Language, Protein Sequence, and Structure with Diffusion Language Models
abstract: We envision a general-purpose protein foundation model as a unified, interactive model of sequence, structure, and function, capable of understanding, generation, and cross-modal translation while retaining the instruction-following and reasoning capabilities of modern LLMs. Toward this vision, we introduce Trion-1, the first native, unified, multimodal diffusion language model (dLLM) for proteins. Trion-1 is built on two key design choices: (1) a unified discrete token space that jointly represents sequence, structure, and natural language; (2) a dLLM backbone that replaces strict left-to-right factorization with bidirectional or semi-bidirectional token interactions, enabling global residue communication and long-range contact modeling that are naturally suited to structure modeling. This formulation unifies six core capabilities: folding, inverse folding, sequence understanding, structure understanding, sequence design, and structure design, while retaining the native language capabilities of general-purpose LLMs. On established benchmarks, Trion-1 achieves broadly competitive performance. In folding, Trion-1 achieves a TM-score above 0.8 with a single sample under strict homology control, matching or exceeding the existing tri-modal model using 200 samples. For sequence understanding, Trion-1 performs on par with top-tier LLMs such as Claude Opus 4.7 (62.37%). These results support well-aligned sequence-structure-language representations and strong cross-modal generative capabilities.

title: Network topology shapes consensus and vulnerability in LLM populations
abstract: As large language models (LLMs) are deployed in interacting populations, their collective behaviour depends not only on the models but also on who interacts with whom. Studies of convention formation in LLM populations have mainly tested well-mixed interactions. We place policies extracted from four LLMs on fully connected, random regular, and heterogeneous networks, with $10^3$ to $10^5$ agents playing the naming game. Topology affects how quickly consensus emerges, sometimes whether it emerges at all, and, in rare cases, which convention wins. Sparsest networks slow consensus up to twelvefold. Yet, by preserving correlations between persistent neighbours, they restore consensus in some cases that fail to converge under well-mixed interactions. Networks also govern vulnerability to adversarial attack. We measure the critical mass of committed agents needed to overturn an established convention. Tipping thresholds follow the same ordering across models and conditions: hubs $\leq$ random $\leq$ low-degree nodes. On the most heterogeneous topology, median critical masses are 3%, 16%, and 35%, respectively; targeting hubs requires one-sixth as many committed agents as random placement. For most models, networked populations are easier to tip than well-mixed ones, so well-mixed estimates can overstate robustness. Assessing the safety of multi-agent AI requires mapping who interacts with whom.

title: GeoAgent: Contract-Constrained LLM Agents for Seismic Data Processing
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can drive scientific software through function calling, but free-form tool use is fragile on long, data-dependent processing chains. Models omit arguments, invent units, feed the previous artifact into the wrong input, and report completion without a verifiable product. We present GeoAgent, an agent system for seismic data processing built on Madagascar's roughly 1{,}965 command-line programs. GeoAgent exposes 54 operator agents (51 generated from a declarative specification), retrieves from an index of 1{,}937 operators, and encodes the processing flow as a nine-stage state graph. Four explicit contracts---named artifacts, input resolution, parameter takeover, and artifact validation---move everything the graph can determine out of the model's discretion. A deterministic geometry tool parses the self-describing SPS/RPS/XPS and SEG-Y headers, cross-checks eight consistency conditions, and reproduces the reference shell recipe exactly. The system runs in containers with session- and task-level isolation, bounded execution, and defenses against silent failures. On a 2-D land dataset, the nine-stage pipeline completes in about six to eleven minutes and yields a verified artifact at every stage, while retrieval reduces per-turn tool context from about 12k to 2k tokens. We report the design, deployment experience, and motivating failure modes.
